overview.text: The 1930s (1930–1939) were a defining decade in U.S. history, shaped by the Great Depression and an expanded federal response. As unemployment, bank failures, foreclosures, and migration strained households and communities, President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal created programs for relief, jobs, farm support, and economic regulation. Its importance lies not only in emergency action: federal involvement in public welfare and economic life grew, and the 1935 Social Security Act established federal old-age benefits alongside unemployment insurance and assistance programs. New Deal laws reached banking, labor, agriculture, public works, and the arts, while political disputes over federal power continued. By the decade’s end, international tensions and debates over isolationism also shaped U.S. politics.

key_facts.text: In 1933, at the Depression’s height, 24.9% of the U.S. workforce was unemployed; many families also faced foreclosure or migrated in search of work.
Roosevelt launched the New Deal after taking office in 1933; its programs included work relief, farm support, and measures affecting industry and banking.
The Civilian Conservation Corps provided jobs for unemployed young people, while the Works Progress Administration funded jobs that included arts projects.
The 1935 Social Security Act established federal old-age benefits and included unemployment insurance and assistance for several groups, including dependent children and people who were blind.
The New Deal expanded federal involvement, but it did not bring complete economic recovery during the 1930s; its policies also faced political opposition.
Late in the decade, Congress debated U.S. involvement in growing international conflicts, with isolationists resisting deeper engagement.
